title: Growing Revenue, Shrinking Cash — Home Décor Retailer
source_basis: common retail working-capital trap pattern
AR/AP timing mismatches documented in SMB lending literature
anonymized composite

scenario.business: Independent home décor retailer, 6 years operating, $2.1M annual revenue, 8 staff. Owner reports growing sales but declining bank balance. Cannot make payroll without a credit line draw three months in a row.
symptoms: owner cannot make payroll without credit line draw
bank balance declining each month despite revenue growth
supplier relationships strained by late payments
owner described feeling confused — sales are up but feels broke
misleading_signals: revenue is up 18% year-over-year and appears healthy
gross margin of 38% looks acceptable for the category
business has been operating profitably on paper for 6 years
missing_inputs_opsiq_should_request: full AR aging report broken down by client and days outstanding
supplier payment terms and flexibility for each major vendor
cash conversion cycle calculation
monthly cash flow statement for past 6 months
concentration of receivables — what percentage is from top 3 clients

expected_opsiq_diagnosis.expected_first_action: Build a 13-week rolling cash flow forecast and map exact AR/AP timing mismatches before any other action.
bad_recommendations_to_flag: increase marketing and sales to grow revenue
hire a sales representative
expand product line to increase order size
take on larger clients to improve revenue
open a second location

must_not_claim: business is fundamentally broken
revenue growth is the problem
gross margin is too low
ideal_depth: quantify the structural timing gap between when supplier payment is due and when client payment arrives
identify the 60-day vs 30-day mismatch as the core structural problem
recommend cash flow forecasting before any growth action
flag credit line as symptom management not solution

title: Inventory Cash Trap — Specialty Outdoor Equipment Retailer
source_basis: seasonal inventory management failure common in specialty retail
working capital trapped in slow-moving SKUs documented pattern
anonymized composite

scenario.business: Specialty outdoor equipment retailer, 9 years operating, $1.4M annual revenue, 5 staff. Owner reports good gross margins but persistent cash shortages. Has both backorders on popular items and excess stock of slow-moving products simultaneously.
symptoms: cash-short every month despite healthy gross margins
backorders on top-selling items while warehouse holds excess slow-moving stock
owner reorders by gut feel not data
seasonal demand spikes create cash crises before season begins
misleading_signals: gross margin of 42% appears healthy for the category
annual revenue is stable and not declining
owner has strong product knowledge and customer relationships
missing_inputs_opsiq_should_request: SKU-level sell-through velocity by category
inventory age by SKU — how long has each unit been held
reorder frequency and minimum order quantities per supplier
cash tied up in top 20 slow-moving SKUs specifically
seasonal demand pattern data by month

expected_opsiq_diagnosis.expected_first_action: Run a full inventory age and velocity analysis by SKU to identify cash locked in slow-moving stock before placing any new orders.
bad_recommendations_to_flag: expand product range to offer more variety
increase marketing spend to move more units
hire more staff to manage inventory
open a second location to reach more customers
take on a business loan to buy more inventory

must_identify: cash tied up in unsold inventory
must_not_claim: gross margin is the problem
business needs more revenue to fix cash
marketing will solve the inventory issue
ideal_depth: identify that cash is structurally locked in slow-moving inventory
explain that expanding the product range worsens the trap
recommend velocity-based reorder logic over gut-feel purchasing
flag simultaneous backorder and overstock as a buying process failure not a demand problem

title: Scaling Losses — DTC Apparel Brand on Paid Acquisition
source_basis: negative unit economics in paid DTC acquisition documented across e-commerce research
blended ROAS masking per-channel contribution margin loss
anonymized composite

scenario.business: Direct-to-consumer apparel brand, 3 years operating, $1.8M annual revenue. Revenue growing 35% year-over-year but owner reports cash disappearing faster as they scale. 30% of revenue attributed to paid social advertising.
symptoms: losses increasing as revenue grows
owner believes more ad spend will solve the profitability problem
contribution margin is negative after accounting for customer acquisition cost
repeat purchase rate is low — most customers buy once
misleading_signals: revenue growing 35% year-over-year looks like strong traction
social media engagement and follower growth are high
gross margin at 44% appears healthy for apparel
missing_inputs_opsiq_should_request: lifetime value by customer cohort broken out by acquisition channel
contribution margin per channel not blended ROAS
repeat purchase rate by acquisition source
cost of goods and fulfillment per order itemized
paid vs organic revenue split and organic growth rate separately

expected_opsiq_diagnosis.expected_first_action: Calculate true contribution margin per order per channel and identify whether any channel has positive unit economics before spending another dollar on paid acquisition.
bad_recommendations_to_flag: increase ad spend to scale revenue
launch more paid campaigns across additional platforms
hire a marketing agency to improve ROAS
grow social media following to improve brand awareness
raise a funding round to fuel paid acquisition

must_identify: paid channel is loss-making at scale
must_not_claim: gross margin alone is sufficient signal
revenue growth validates the business model
social engagement proves product market fit
ideal_depth: identify that blended ROAS masks per-channel contribution
explain that scaling a negative-margin channel destroys cash faster
quantify the structural CAC-LTV gap
flag low repeat rate as compounding the acquisition dependency problem

title: Always Busy, Never Profitable — Independent Casual Dining Restaurant
source_basis: prime cost management failure common in independent restaurant failures
food and labor cost mismanagement documented in restaurant industry benchmarks
anonymized composite

scenario.business: Independent casual dining restaurant, 7 years operating, $1.2M annual revenue, 18 staff including kitchen and front-of-house. Owner reports the restaurant is consistently busy but money never accumulates. Net income near zero despite high seat occupancy.
symptoms: restaurant full on weekends but no profit accumulating
owner taking no salary for past 6 months
food waste observed but not tracked systematically
kitchen staff scheduling is reactive not planned
misleading_signals: weekend occupancy is 92% — looks like demand is not the problem
revenue is stable at $1.2M with no major decline
customer reviews are positive and return visits are common
missing_inputs_opsiq_should_request: weekly prime cost tracking data — current prime cost is estimated not measured
food cost percentage by menu item or category
labor cost breakdown by role and shift
food waste tracking log
menu engineering analysis — which items have highest margin vs popularity

expected_opsiq_diagnosis.expected_first_action: Implement weekly prime cost tracking immediately — calculate combined food and labor cost as a percentage of weekly revenue and establish a target below 65%.
bad_recommendations_to_flag: advertise more to bring in additional customers
add more seating capacity to increase revenue
increase table turns to serve more covers
open for more hours to grow revenue
hire more kitchen staff to improve service speed

must_not_claim: restaurant needs more customers to be profitable
marketing will fix the margin problem
the business model is fundamentally broken
ideal_depth: identify that prime cost at 68% exceeds the 60-65% industry benchmark
explain that more revenue without fixing prime cost worsens the cash position
recommend weekly prime cost tracking as the first control mechanism
flag that busy occupancy is a misleading signal masking the margin structure problem

title: One Client Owns the Business — B2B Marketing Agency
source_basis: revenue concentration risk in professional services documented in SMB survival literature
single-client dependency creating existential fragility
anonymized composite

scenario.business: Two-person B2B marketing agency, 4 years operating, $380K annual revenue. One client accounts for 74% of revenue on a month-to-month retainer. Owner avoids investing in systems, hiring, or expansion due to anxiety about losing the main client.
symptoms: owner cannot sleep when primary client seems unhappy
no new business development happening
any staffing or investment decision feels too risky
owner has avoided raising rates for fear of losing primary client
misleading_signals: revenue appears stable and profitable at $380K
primary client relationship seems strong after 4 years
owner has deep expertise and strong client satisfaction
missing_inputs_opsiq_should_request: contract renewal probability assessment — has renewal been discussed
current secondary client pipeline and conversion rate
pricing headroom — has the owner tested rate increases with any client
time allocation between client delivery and business development
primary client NPS or satisfaction signals

expected_opsiq_diagnosis.expected_first_action: Quantify concentration risk and begin a structured minimum 10% time allocation to new business development regardless of primary client demand.
bad_recommendations_to_flag: hire more staff immediately to scale capacity
invest in office space or tooling
launch new service lines to diversify
increase ad spend or content marketing
immediately raise rates on the primary client as first action

must_not_claim: business is performing well and just needs growth
four-year relationship guarantees renewal
hiring will solve the concentration problem
ideal_depth: identify that month-to-month contract plus 74% concentration equals existential risk
explain that owner paralysis is a rational response to real structural fragility
recommend pipeline development before any capacity or investment expansion
flag that stable revenue appearance masks the underlying concentration exposure

title: Fixed Cost Overextension — Independent Fitness Studio
source_basis: fixed cost overextension below breakeven documented in fitness industry failure patterns
lease burden relative to revenue common SMB failure mode
anonymized composite

scenario.business: Independent fitness studio, 2.5 years operating, $35K average monthly revenue, 3 staff. Owner signed a 5-year lease at $28K/month in month 6 of operations. Now running monthly losses and drawing personal savings.
symptoms: monthly losses of approximately $13K per month
owner drawing personal savings to cover operations
member count growth has stalled below breakeven
owner focused on adding more classes to increase revenue
misleading_signals: member NPS is 72 — very high satisfaction
social media reviews are strong
owner correctly identifies that adding members would fix the issue but has not fixed the structural gap
missing_inputs_opsiq_should_request: member churn rate and reason for leaving
variable cost per member enrolled
breakeven member count calculation
lease flexibility or subletting options
member acquisition cost and conversion rate from trial

expected_opsiq_diagnosis.expected_first_action: Calculate exact breakeven member count required to cover fixed costs and assess whether that number is achievable given current trial conversion and market size before adding any new programs.
bad_recommendations_to_flag: launch more classes to increase revenue
increase social media advertising
hire another trainer to expand capacity
open a second location
add premium services to increase revenue per member

must_identify: fixed costs exceed revenue at current volume
must_not_claim: NPS score means the business is viable
adding more classes solves the structural problem
the fix is purely a marketing problem
ideal_depth: identify that fixed costs of $48K against $35K revenue is structural not operational
explain that adding classes or marketing does not change the fixed cost structure
calculate or reference the breakeven gap
flag that personal savings draw is the danger signal of runway consumption

title: Capacity Ceiling — Solopreneur HR Consultant
source_basis: owner-operator capacity ceiling as revenue ceiling documented in solopreneur business literature
leverage gap preventing growth at personal capacity
anonymized composite

scenario.business: Independent HR consultant, 6 years in business, $318K annual revenue, billing 35 client hours per week at $175/hour. Has a waitlist of potential clients. Owner working 60+ total hours weekly including admin, proposal writing, and bookkeeping. Reports declining quality on some engagements.
symptoms: cannot accept waitlisted clients without sacrificing quality on existing clients
quality of work declining as hours increase
owner experiencing burnout signals
revenue has been flat for 18 months despite strong demand
misleading_signals: business appears successful — waitlist and strong rate suggests demand is not the problem
revenue of $318K appears healthy for a solo operator
strong client retention masks the structural ceiling
missing_inputs_opsiq_should_request: breakdown of non-billable hours by activity — what admin tasks consume the most time
whether any task could be systematized or delegated to a VA or junior hire
whether the owner has tested a rate increase to reduce hours while maintaining revenue
leverage options explored — associates, white-label partnerships, group programs
owner target for personal working hours and income

expected_opsiq_diagnosis.expected_first_action: Map all 27 non-billable hours by activity and identify which can be eliminated, systematized, or delegated — before considering hiring or rate changes.
bad_recommendations_to_flag: work harder to serve more clients
take on more clients by adding more hours
hire a junior consultant immediately and bill them out
immediately raise rates to $300 per hour without testing
launch a digital product or course as the first action

must_identify: revenue ceiling tied to personal hours
must_not_claim: the business needs more marketing
revenue is insufficient and needs to be grown through new clients
hiring is the immediate first step
ideal_depth: identify that revenue ceiling is structurally tied to owner hours
explain that adding clients without creating leverage worsens quality
recommend admin time audit as the first intervention not hiring
flag that waitlist is a lever only if capacity is unlocked

title: Revenue on Paper, Cash in the Void — IT Managed Services Provider
source_basis: accounts receivable cash flow gap documented in B2B services SMB literature
DSO above 45 days creating structural cash deficit in small MSPs
anonymized composite

scenario.business: IT managed services provider, 5 years operating, 12 contracted SMB clients, $95K monthly recurring revenue billed. Owner reports negative monthly cash flow despite strong contract base. Drawing personal credit to fund operations.
symptoms: $27K monthly gap between billed and collected revenue
three clients have unpaid invoices over 90 days
owner personally financing operations with personal credit
invoices sent but follow-up collection process is informal and inconsistent
misleading_signals: contracted MRR of $95K appears strong and growing
client relationships seem good — no one has explicitly said they are unhappy
low churn rate of 8% suggests clients value the service
missing_inputs_opsiq_should_request: AR aging report broken down by client — which clients are 30, 60, 90+ days
contractual payment terms — do contracts specify payment deadlines and late fees
current collection process documentation — what happens after invoice is sent
whether late-paying clients have been formally notified or placed on service terms review
personal credit terms and runway remaining

expected_opsiq_diagnosis.expected_first_action: Produce an AR aging report by client, identify the three 90+ day accounts, and initiate formal collection actions with documented escalation steps within one week.
bad_recommendations_to_flag: acquire more clients to increase revenue
expand service offering to add revenue streams
hire a sales representative
invest in marketing to grow the client base
raise pricing to improve cash flow

must_not_claim: business needs more clients to solve cash problem
marketing will fix the cash gap
low churn rate means the business is healthy
ideal_depth: identify DSO of 47 days as the structural problem not revenue
explain that growing client count without fixing collections worsens the gap
recommend AR aging analysis and formal collection process as the immediate action
flag that personal credit draw is a runway signal requiring urgent action

title: Turnover Spiral — Residential and Commercial Cleaning Business
source_basis: staff turnover cost spiral documented in labor-intensive SMB service businesses
retention-recruitment cycle destroying margins common in cleaning industry
anonymized composite

scenario.business: Residential and commercial cleaning business, 11 years operating, 8 field staff, $620K annual revenue. Owner reports chronic understaffing, declining service quality, and loss of commercial contracts. Spends 12 hours per week on recruiting.
symptoms: 3 open positions at any given time consuming owner time
service quality complaints increasing as undertrained staff fill gaps
lost 3 commercial contracts citing inconsistent service quality
owner cannot focus on growth because of constant recruiting and training
misleading_signals: revenue appears roughly flat — not visibly declining
demand for cleaning services remains high in the local market
owner interprets turnover as normal for the industry
missing_inputs_opsiq_should_request: exit interview data — why do staff leave within 6 months
compensation benchmarks versus competing employers in the local market
onboarding and training process documentation
current wages compared to local competitors in cleaning and adjacent service businesses
whether any incentive or tenure bonus structure exists

expected_opsiq_diagnosis.expected_first_action: Conduct immediate exit interview analysis of last 10 departures and run a local wage benchmarking exercise before next hire to identify whether compensation is the primary attrition driver.
bad_recommendations_to_flag: hire more staff immediately to fill open positions
increase marketing to win more commercial contracts while understaffed
invest in equipment or technology
expand service area to generate more revenue
launch a referral program to acquire more residential clients

must_not_claim: business needs more revenue to solve the turnover problem
marketing will stabilize the business
turnover is unavoidable in this industry
ideal_depth: identify that 140% turnover rate is the structural cost driver not just an operational inconvenience
calculate or reference the annualized cost of turnover at $1,800 per hire times frequency
explain that winning more contracts while understaffed accelerates the spiral
recommend root cause diagnosis of exit data before any hiring action

title: Input Cost Squeeze With Frozen Prices — Two-Location Artisan Bakery
source_basis: commodity cost pass-through failure common in independent food businesses
owner fear of raising prices despite margin compression documented
anonymized composite

scenario.business: Two-location artisan bakery, 8 years operating, $890K combined annual revenue. Owner reports working harder every year but earning less. Input costs have increased sharply over 18 months. Prices have not been adjusted in two years.
symptoms: gross margin dropped from 41% to 28% over 18 months without any pricing response
owner working same or more hours for significantly less net income
fear of raising prices driving continued margin compression
no data on what price increase the market will actually tolerate
misleading_signals: revenue is holding steady — customer volume has not declined
loyal customer base and positive community reputation
owner interprets stable revenue as evidence that prices cannot be raised
missing_inputs_opsiq_should_request: competitor pricing survey — what are comparable bakeries charging for similar items
menu engineering analysis — gross margin and volume by individual menu item
customer price sensitivity data — has any price testing ever been done
current commodity cost trajectory — are costs still rising or stabilizing
which menu items have the highest margin and which are below breakeven

expected_opsiq_diagnosis.expected_first_action: Run a menu engineering analysis to identify the highest-margin and lowest-margin items, then test a targeted price increase on 3-5 key items to measure actual customer price sensitivity before generalizing.
bad_recommendations_to_flag: reduce prices to compete with larger bakeries
add more SKUs or menu items to spread fixed cost
open a third location to increase revenue
invest in marketing and social media to attract more customers
cut staff to reduce labor cost as the primary action

must_identify: price has not been raised despite cost increase
must_not_claim: stable revenue means prices cannot be raised
customer loyalty prevents any price increases
marketing will solve the margin compression
ideal_depth: identify that 13-point margin compression is driven by input cost not demand failure
explain that stable revenue with unchanged prices is not evidence of price sensitivity
recommend price testing before accepting the assumption that customers will not accept increases
flag that adding a third location accelerates cash drain without fixing margin structure

title: Audience Without Revenue — Creator-Turned-SaaS Productivity Tool
source_basis: vanity metric product market fit gap documented in bootstrapped SaaS literature
audience engagement and paid conversion divergence common in creator-led products
anonymized composite

scenario.business: Solo founder, 8 months post-launch of a productivity tool for freelancers built on top of an existing newsletter audience. 12,000 newsletter subscribers, 4,200 free tool users, 2.1% paid conversion rate, $47 MRR. Founder assumes paid conversion will grow as audience grows.
symptoms: MRR of $47 after 8 months with 12K engaged audience members
2.1% paid conversion rate — most engaged users never convert to paid
founder attributes low paid conversion to needing a larger audience
no systematic effort to understand why free users do not pay
misleading_signals: 38% email open rate is unusually high and signals genuine audience engagement
4,200 free tool users shows the product gets adoption
strong social following reinforces the founder confidence in audience quality
missing_inputs_opsiq_should_request: exit survey or interview data from users who tried the free tool and did not convert to paid
willingness-to-pay research — have any interviews been done asking what users would pay and for what
job-to-be-done analysis — is the tool solving a pain users currently pay to solve elsewhere
churn rate of paying users — are the 88 paid users retaining
what specific feature or outcome prompted the 88 users who did pay to convert

expected_opsiq_diagnosis.expected_first_action: Interview 10 free users who have not converted and 5 users who have paid to map the specific job-to-be-done and willingness-to-pay gap before any audience growth or feature investment.
bad_recommendations_to_flag: grow social media following to increase potential conversion pool
increase content output and posting frequency
launch an affiliate program to drive more signups
add more features to make the free tier more compelling
raise funding based on audience engagement metrics

must_identify: audience engagement is not the same as willingness to pay
must_not_claim: audience size and engagement validates the business model
more signups will naturally lead to more paid conversions
the tool just needs more time to grow
ideal_depth: identify that audience engagement and paid conversion are distinct and currently divergent
explain that growing a free audience without understanding the conversion gap compounds the problem
recommend qualitative paid conversion diagnosis before any growth action
flag that 2.1% paid conversion after 8 months requires diagnosis not more traffic

title: Premature Expansion — Multi-Location Tutoring Center
source_basis: unit economics failure in premature multi-location expansion documented in education SMB literature
profitable original location subsidizing unproven expansion sites
anonymized composite

scenario.business: Owner-operated tutoring center chain, 3 locations. Location 1 (4 years): established, profitable. Locations 2 and 3 opened to capitalize on brand success. Owner planning a 4th location citing network effects. Monthly financials show aggregate loss.
symptoms: locations 2 and 3 are loss-making 18 months and 6 months in respectively
original profitable location is subsidizing two expansion sites
owner is planning a 4th location without fixing unit economics at locations 2 and 3
combined monthly loss despite strong original location performance
misleading_signals: total enrollment across all locations is growing — looks like growth story
strong brand in local market and positive parent reviews
owner network effect theory sounds plausible without per-location P&L scrutiny
missing_inputs_opsiq_should_request: per-location full P&L not just contribution margin
enrollment rate as a percentage of capacity per location
breakeven enrollment count per location
lead generation and conversion rate by location — are locations 2 and 3 in addressable markets
what the 18-month trajectory looks like for location 2 — is it improving or flat

expected_opsiq_diagnosis.expected_first_action: Freeze location 4 planning and run a full per-location P&L to determine whether location 2 is on a path to breakeven before committing any additional capital to expansion.
bad_recommendations_to_flag: open more locations to create network effects
increase marketing spend across all locations to drive enrollment
hire more tutors to increase capacity at locations 2 and 3
launch online tutoring to add a revenue stream
take a business loan to fund location 4

must_identify: premature expansion before unit economics proven
must_not_claim: total enrollment growth validates the expansion strategy
network effects justify opening location 4
more marketing will fix the unit economics
ideal_depth: identify that location 1 profitability does not validate locations 2 and 3
explain that opening location 4 while 2 and 3 are loss-making worsens cash drain
recommend per-location breakeven analysis and freeze on expansion before any growth action
flag that aggregate enrollment growth is a vanity metric masking per-location economics
